newsitem.title: KENYA: Human rights group says Rwanda massacres rise.
newsitem.headline: Human rights group says Rwanda massacres rise.

text.p: The human rights group Amnesty International said on Thursday massacres of civilians in Rwanda had increased since May and accused the international community of ignoring the slaughter.
The London-based human rights group said in May, June and July more than 2,300 unarmed civilians were estimated killed.
It said among the victims were Rwandan Hutu refugees who had returned from the former Zaire after their refugee camps were attacked by Tutsi-dominated rebel forces which captured Kinshasa in May.

"Given the persistent and grave human rights violations taking place in Rwanda, it cannot be considered safe for refugees to return," said Amnesty, adding "the international community looks the other way" despite killings escalating.

The Rwandan government has said the group's previous reports of killings in Rwanda were exaggerated and inaccurate but says some civilians have been killed in crossfire between troops and Hutu rebels.

"The organisation is receiving daily reports of killings of men, women and young children by soldiers of the Rwandan Patriotic Army (RPA), especially in the northwestern regions of Ruhengeri and Gisenyi, which have become virtual no-go areas.

"Armed opposition groups believed to be composed of soldiers of the former Rwandan army and militia responsible for the genocide of 1994 are also carrying out attacks on civilians as well as RPA personnel," it said.

"Testimonies from these regions consistently affirm that most of the victims of the violence in recent months have died at the hands of the RPA, especially during military cordon and search operations," it said.
It added these operations were usually launched by the government army after attacks by armed opposition groups.

"Counter-insurgency operations can never be a justification for the army to extrajudicially execute unarmed civilians," Amnesty said. "Contrary to what the government sometimes claims, these victims are not killed accidentally in cross-fire."
"Whole families, including many children, have been hunted down in their homes," it said.
Amnesty said although the government had said it was investigating the killings it had failed to publish results.
It said hundreds of people and possibly as many as 955 were killed in the western prefecture of Gisenyi in June and July and all the killings were attributed by local sources to the RPA.
It cited six other massacres ranging from 16 to more than 520 people each by RPA troops and Hutu rebels from May to July.
An estimated 800,000 Hutus and Tutsi moderates were killed by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs in genocide in 1994 until Tutsi-dominated rebels seized the country and became the new national army.
